The Bregman-divergence framework

framework.Rmd

Every estimator in BregSurv minimizes the same objective. This page sets out that objective, shows how it separates three decisions that methods for borrowing external information usually tie together, and maps each combination to what the package fits. Get started shows the calls.

Two cohorts, one objective

You have a target cohort, your own time-to-event data, and an external source: a registry, a published model, another study. The external source decides what it releases: individual records, fitted coefficients with their uncertainty, or only a fitted model. Its population may differ from yours, so borrowing must be tunable, and must be able to switch off.

With \(\ell(\theta)\) the target log-likelihood, every estimator minimizes

\[ Q_\eta(\theta) \;=\; -\ell(\theta) \;+\; \eta\,\mathcal{B}_G(\theta), \qquad \eta \ge 0, \]

where \(\mathcal{B}_G\) is a Bregman divergence between the target model and the external one, \(B_G(\mathbf u \,\|\, \mathbf v) = G(\mathbf u) - G(\mathbf v) - \nabla G(\mathbf v)^\top(\mathbf u - \mathbf v)\), for a strictly convex generator \(G\).

  • The integration weight \(\eta\) sets how strongly to borrow. At \(\eta = 0\) the fit is the target model alone; as \(\eta\) grows, the fit is pulled toward the external model. cv.bregsurv() chooses \(\eta\) by cross-validation on the target data.
  • The generator \(G\) sets the geometry of the borrowing, and is fixed by what the external source released.

The objective separates three decisions, made by three different parties, and the package has an object for each:

decision made by cv.bregsurv() argument
the target model the analyst, from the data and the question target = target_cox(...), target_ncc(...), target_discrete(...), linear or nn_score()
the form of the release the external source release = release_records(...), release_coef(...), release_score(...), release_model(...)
how the release enters, and how strongly the analyst and the target data, by cross-validation divergence = ..., and the chosen eta

The release decides the divergence

what the external source released generator \(G\) divergence divergence =
individual-level records \(-\ell_{\text{ext}}\), the external log-likelihood composite likelihood "composite"
coefficients with their uncertainty \(\tfrac12 \mathbf u^\top A \mathbf u\) Mahalanobis distance to \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\) "mahalanobis"
a fitted model or risk score alone negative entropy on the model’s conditional distributions Kullback–Leibler divergence "kl"

Individual-level records. With \(G = -\ell_{\text{ext}}\) the objective becomes, up to a constant, \(-\ell(\theta) - \eta\,\ell_{\text{ext}}(\theta)\): a weighted fit to the stacked cohorts in which each cohort keeps its own baseline and the external events carry weight \(\eta\).

Coefficients with their uncertainty. The penalty is \(\tfrac12(\boldsymbol\beta - \tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top A\,(\boldsymbol\beta - \tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})\), with \(A\) a precision matrix: the external information matrix, the inverse of a reported covariance, or a diagonal of inverse variances when only standard errors were published. Without one, \(A\) is the identity on the covariates the external model covers and zero elsewhere, a Euclidean distance. When \(A\) is the observed information, this penalty is the second-order approximation of the composite likelihood around \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\).

A fitted model or risk score alone. The two models are compared through the conditional distributions they induce: on a Cox target, which member of each risk set fails; on a discrete target, whether each subject at risk fails in each interval. The Kullback–Leibler divergence between them reduces the objective to the target likelihood with each outcome replaced by a blend of the observed outcome and the external model’s prediction, \((\delta + \eta\,\tilde\delta)/(1+\eta)\). On a Cox target the external model enters only through its risk score, which may come from a model of any form and may use only part of your covariates; on a discrete target it enters through its absolute risk, the interval hazards.

The three forms are levels of access, not rival methods. Records yield coefficients and a precision matrix, and coefficients yield a risk score, so a release enters at its own level and every level below it, and cross-validation on the target data decides which divergence borrows best.

What the target can be

target constructor likelihood divergences
Cox model target_cox() stratified partial likelihood; ties = "breslow" or "exact" for tied times all three
Nested case–control design target_ncc() conditional likelihood of the case within its matched set all three
Discrete-time model target_discrete() grouped-time Bernoulli likelihood, complementary log-log or logit link all three
Neural network (Cox or discrete) score = nn_score() the same likelihoods, with a network risk score Kullback–Leibler

Every linear target takes penalty = "ridge", "lasso" or "enet"; the penalty path is built for each \(\eta\) separately. coxkl_enet.multi() combines several external sources, each with its own weight.

Choosing what to borrow and how strongly

cv.bregsurv() uses a fixed seed by default, and the fold assignment depends only on the seed, the events and the strata. Fits to the same target are therefore scored on the same partition by the same criterion, and their values compare directly:

target criterion
Cox, linear or neural cross-validated partial-likelihood loss of Verweij and Van Houwelingen
nested case–control cross-validated conditional-likelihood loss
discrete time, linear or neural held-out negative log-likelihood per subject, pooled over the folds

The two endpoints that borrow nothing belong in the same comparison: the target model alone (cv.bregsurv(target)), and, on a Cox target, the external model used unchanged (vvh_loss_fixed() on the same folds).

library(BregSurv)
data(ExampleData_lowdim)
tr <- ExampleData_lowdim$train
target  <- target_cox(tr$time, tr$status, tr$z)
release <- release_coef(ExampleData_lowdim$beta_external_fair)

fits <- list(kullback_leibler = cv.bregsurv(target, release, divergence = "kl"),
             euclidean        = cv.bregsurv(target, release, divergence = "mahalanobis"),
             kl_lasso         = cv.bregsurv(target, release, divergence = "kl", penalty = "lasso"),
             target_only      = cv.bregsurv(target))
as_is <- vvh_loss_fixed(as.matrix(tr$z), tr$status, tr$time,
                        beta = ExampleData_lowdim$beta_external_fair, folds = fits[[1]]$folds)
c(sapply(fits, `[[`, "value"), external_as_is = as_is$VVH_Loss)

This is how the agent in this repository works: it fits every divergence the facts admit, on one partition, and selects by that number.

Where each call goes

On a linear target cv.bregsurv() calls one of the package’s estimators and returns its result unchanged; the engine field of the result names the one used. The three designs have parallel families of estimators, one per divergence.

target divergence no penalty ridge lasso / elastic net
Cox composite cv.cox_indi cv.cox_indi_ridge cv.cox_indi_enet
Cox Mahalanobis cv.cox_MDTL cv.cox_MDTL_ridge cv.cox_MDTL_enet
Cox Kullback–Leibler cv.coxkl (cv.coxkl_ties for exact ties) cv.coxkl_ridge cv.coxkl_enet
nested case–control composite cv.ncc_indi – cv.ncc_indi_enet
nested case–control Mahalanobis cv.ncc_MDTL cv.ncc_MDTL_ridge cv.ncc_MDTL_enet
nested case–control Kullback–Leibler cv.ncckl cv.ncckl_ridge cv.ncckl_enet
discrete time composite cv.discrete_indi cv.discrete_indi_ridge cv.discrete_indi_enet
discrete time Mahalanobis cv.discrete_MDTL cv.discrete_MDTL_ridge cv.discrete_MDTL_enet
discrete time Kullback–Leibler cv.discretekl cv.discretekl_ridge cv.discretekl_enet
neural network Kullback–Leibler torch

Each cv. function has a counterpart without the prefix that fits at given weights (coxkl(), discrete_MDTL(), …). The estimators behind each divergence walks through them with all their options.
